summary: You produced a correct brute-force solution for standard cases and were careful to avoid using the same element twice by starting the inner loop at i+1. However, you missed an explicit behavior expected by the tests for empty/no-solution inputs (return [] instead of raising), and you did not move to the expected O(n) hash-map solution given the input size constraints.

test_results.summary_note: Most tests passed, but an edge-case test expected [] on empty input while the solution raised ValueError.

dimensions.name: Correctness & Completeness
dimensions.label: adequate
dimensions.what_went_well: Core logic finds a valid pair and correctly avoids reusing the same index by iterating j from i+1.
dimensions.what_to_improve: Match the required output contract for edge cases: return [] (or otherwise specified sentinel) rather than raising on empty/no-solution inputs, since the test suite explicitly checks this.

dimensions.name: Problem-Solving & Thinking
dimensions.label: adequate
dimensions.what_went_well: You started with a straightforward baseline, validated it on examples, and demonstrated awareness that a hash map approach exists for optimization.
dimensions.what_to_improve: When constraints allow n up to 1e5, treat optimization as part of the core solution plan: articulate the hash-map invariant (seen value -> index; check complement first) and implement it early rather than leaving it as a “if time” improvement.

dimensions.name: Technical Communication
dimensions.label: adequate
dimensions.what_went_well: Your restatement was accurate (two distinct indices) and you clearly described loop bounds and the resulting time/space complexity.
dimensions.what_to_improve: Explicitly confirm assumptions against requirements/tests before submitting (e.g., whether empty input/no-solution can appear despite typical Two Sum constraints), and state the intended behavior in those cases.

dimensions.name: Complexity & Optimization
dimensions.label: needs work
dimensions.what_went_well: You correctly identified the brute-force complexity as O(n^2) time and O(1) space, and you knew the optimal hash-map direction.
dimensions.what_to_improve: Implement the canonical O(n) single-pass hash-map solution when n can be 1e5; O(n^2) will not scale and is specifically called out as a known pitfall in the answer key.

dimensions.name: Code Quality
dimensions.label: adequate
dimensions.what_went_well: Code is simple, readable, and uses correct iteration boundaries to prevent index reuse.
dimensions.what_to_improve: Avoid using exceptions for normal control flow in interview settings unless required; return a defined value (like []) and add a small guard clause at the top for empty inputs.

dimensions.name: Independence
dimensions.label: needs work
dimensions.what_went_well: You built a working baseline solution without needing step-by-step guidance.
dimensions.what_to_improve: Act on general prompts about edge cases before submitting—here, the hint to consider unusual inputs did not translate into adding/adjusting behavior for empty input/no-solution.

primary_focus: Internalize and default to the single-pass hash-map Two Sum pattern (check complement before insert) so you consistently hit O(n) and still handle edge-case output contracts like empty input.
thinking_and_logic: You approached the problem by enumerating all pairs (i, j) with i < j and returning the first pair that sums to target, which is logically sound for finding a valid answer and avoids using the same element twice. The gap was in aligning assumptions with the test contract: despite typical constraints implying an answer exists, the tests included an empty-input case expecting [] rather than an exception. You also explicitly recognized the O(n) hash-map approach but did not implement it within the timebox, leaving the solution at O(n^2).
code_assessment: Your final code is the answer key’s brute-force approach (nested loops), achieving O(n^2) time and O(1) space. The canonical optimal solution you missed is the single-pass hash map (value -> index) that checks for the complement before inserting the current value, yielding O(n) time and O(n) space and scaling to n = 1e5. Additionally, your function raises on no-solution/empty input, but the tests expected returning an empty list; the optimal/canonical approach can still return [] when no pair is found (or if nums is empty) instead of throwing.

next_steps.action: Implement the canonical single-pass hash-map Two Sum solution from memory (seen: value->index; if target-x in seen return [seen[target-x], i]; else seen[x]=i).
next_steps.why: This is the expected interview solution for large constraints and fixes the scalability issue versus O(n^2).
next_steps.how: Practice writing it in <5 minutes, then test on cases with duplicates (e.g., nums=[3,3], target=6), negatives, and large arrays; ensure you check complement before insert to avoid using the same index.

next_steps.action: Adopt a quick pre-submit checklist for edge cases and output contracts (empty input, no-solution behavior, duplicates).
next_steps.why: You lost points on an edge-case expectation (return [] vs raising) even though the core logic was fine.
next_steps.how: Before submitting, run through: (1) what happens if nums is empty? (2) what if no pair exists? (3) what’s the required return type/value in those cases? Then encode that as a guard clause and a final return [].

next_steps.action: Practice the sorted-array follow-up variant using the two-pointer pattern.
next_steps.why: It’s a common extension and reinforces choosing the right pattern based on input properties.
next_steps.how: Solve: given sorted nums, move l/r based on sum vs target; track indices carefully; aim for O(n) time, O(1) extra space.

patterns_to_study: single-pass hash map (complement lookup) for Two Sum
encouragement: You have the fundamentals (correct baseline, correct complexity analysis, awareness of the optimal approach); converting that awareness into consistently implementing the O(n) hash-map pattern and tightening edge-case handling will noticeably improve your interview performance.

transcript.text: Here's the problem: given an array of integers and a target, return the indices of the two numbers that add up to the target.
Let me restate: I need two distinct indices whose values sum to the target. I'll start with the straightforward approach — check every pair with two loops — and optimize if there's time.
Writing the nested loops now. Outer loop i, inner loop from i plus one so I don't reuse the same element.
Okay, it works on the example. Running the visible tests.
Before you finish — consider whether there are any unusual inputs worth checking.
Unusual inputs... duplicates should be fine since I use indices. I think I'm good, submitting.
One of the visible tests failed — the empty input case. You raised an error instead of returning an empty list.
Ah, I see. I assumed there's always a solution because of the constraints, so I raised. I'd need a guard for empty or no-solution inputs.
What's the complexity of your solution?
Two nested loops, so O(n squared) time and constant space. I know a hash map would make it O(n) but I didn't get to it.
